title: Scientists Made a Mini Black Hole Out of Light!
summary: Have you ever wondered what it would be like to hold a black hole in your hand? Well, scientists didn't quite do that, but they did something almost as cool: they made a tiny black hole out of light! It's not the kind that sucks in planets—it's a pretend one that follows the same rules. And for the first time, they saw it glow with a special light called Hawking radiation. Stephen Hawking, a famous physicist, predicted this glow back in 1974. He said real black holes should leak a faint heat, but it's so weak we can't see it from Earth. So, researchers built a mini version using a thin glass fiber, like the ones that carry internet. They shot a super-fast, bright pulse of light through the fiber. This pulse changed how the glass bent light, making a moving 'speed bump.' Then they sent a second, weaker pulse. When it hit the bump, it couldn't keep up—and that created a pretend black hole horizon, a point of no return. The magic happened in ultraviolet light. Hawking radiation comes in pairs: one escapes, and the other falls in. In the fiber, the 'falling' part showed up as ultraviolet light with a wavelength of 233 nanometers—that's tinier than the smallest scale in nature! The team counted these photons and saw the glow had a temperature, just like Hawking said. But here's the really new part: they saw the black hole lose a tiny bit of energy. Making the glow nudged the original light pulse, shifting its color a little. That's the 'back reaction'—the black hole paying for its own shine. Over a very, very long time, this would make a real black hole evaporate. This experiment helps scientists understand how the universe's biggest mysteries—quantum physics and gravity—might fit together. And it all happened on a tabletop!
why_it_matters: Learning how tiny light pulses can act like a black hole helps scientists answer big questions about the universe, which could lead to amazing inventions in the future, just like understanding electricity gave us light bulbs.

background_read: Stephen Hawking (a famous British physicist who used a wheelchair) predicted in 1974 that black holes aren't completely black but give off a faint heat called Hawking radiation.
Real black holes are too far away to see this glow, so scientists have tried for decades to build pretend ones in labs.
This new experiment is the first to show the glow and also how it makes the black hole lose a tiny bit of energy, helping us understand how the universe works at its smallest and biggest levels.
Article_Structure: WHO: Researchers studying quantum physics and black holes.
WHAT: Created a pretend black hole using light pulses in a glass fiber, observed Hawking radiation in ultraviolet light, and saw a back reaction that made the black hole lose energy.
WHERE: In a laboratory on a tabletop using a thin glass fiber.
WHY: To test Stephen Hawking's prediction and help connect the rules of tiny particles (quantum physics) with the force of gravity.

perspectives.description: This experiment shows that Hawking's prediction was right and that black holes do lose energy. It's a huge step toward solving a big mystery in physics.
Some people might say it's only a pretend black hole made of light, not a real one in space, so it might not tell us everything about real black holes.
Other scientists are just eager to learn more. This tabletop setup is a new way to study the rules of the universe without needing a spaceship.
